summary: Retired directions still cost CPU, disk, CI and review time in both repositories: an episode-compilation collector alone burns about 3.9 CPU-hours a day collecting nothing, retired lanes hold 67 GiB, and an unused beta-cohort check can roll back any WebApp deploy. The trial cannot be deleted by name, because 17 of its 59 live imports are generic helpers the simulation build needs; the report gives a seven-PR cut order. The job-evidence panel, the staff captures page and two worker lanes form chains with zero production records and can go. The prize is roughly 95,000 Pipeline lines and 27,000 WebApp lines of source, about 140 test files, 16 shipped unit files plus 229 host-only units, 4 WebApp packages and 3 Pipeline dependency groups.

findings.today: Each family is several times what the core loop needs (table in the report). The cost is CI minutes, review time and the chance that a change breaks a part no one uses.
findings.should: Each family sized to the core loop plus the three hard stops.
findings.proposal: Work the delete list in raw/delete-candidates.md in order; then cap each family in CI (for example a check that fails when a new env name or collection appears without an owner line).
findings.user_result: Faster changes to the job path.
findings.risk: Deleting by count is not the goal; each candidate carries its own check.

CI minutes are estimated from six sampled runs per workflow over 7 days, not from billing.
Journey E (investor demo) was not yet written when this report was finished; its findings are not cross-referenced.
Cloud Run, GCP and B2 objects held by retired lanes were not inventoried (door only sees the host).
I did not run any test suite; deletion safety claims rest on the import graph and string search, not on a green build after deletion.
The spend guard costs about 35 CPU-seconds per run (about 8.7 CPU-hours a day); I did not measure how much of that is the RunPod query.
